years. In that time he has won
the Badger Midget Racing asso-

and has scored many wins in
United States Auto Club midget

of cars including one owned by

driver and owner. Wood, who
weighs 150 pounds or so, has the

KEITH THOMAS
Madison, Wis.
Keith Thomas has been driving midget autos,
mostly on the Badger Midget Racing circuit, since
1951. He was champion of the Badger group for the
1961 and 1962 seasons. Tried his hand at sprint car
racing but had a couple of accidents and near acci-
dents, then switched his full attention back to the
small cars. Qualified for the 1959, 100 mile United
States Auto Club midget auto race here on the big
track, finishing 19th, competing against the best in
the midget auto racing sport. Thomas drives a car
sponsored by Paul Krueger of Madison, Wis.

MEL CORNETT
Two products of the rough, tough modified stock car racing circuit in southeastern Wisconsin who have
turned to midget auto racing with success are Dick Schetter and Mel Cornet, both of Milwaukee.
Schetter, who operates a Mobil service station at 683 S. Hawley road, started driving modified stock cars
in 1961, the same year Cornett broke into the sport. Both had varying degrees of success and more than their
share of bad breaks.
Last year was Schetter's first in midget auto racing, and Cornett's third. Schetter won a feature and a
number of preliminary events. Cornett also took the checkered flag in several races.
Cornett ranked 10th in the last published Badger Midget standings, while Schetter, plagued by a string
of mechanical troubles, ranked 24th.

JOHN HARTWIG, Watertown
One Sunday night in 1957, Duane Hanson flipped his midget racing car in a time trial run at Sun Prairie.
As he lay on the ground, the track physician, while working on him, asked "young man, what happened?"
'I don't know, doctor," Hanson answered, "but I'm sorry if I'm making any trouble for you." That typifies
Duane Hanson, a veteran of 18 years in midget racing who was born in Stoughton. A gentle, considerate person
unlike the prototype of race driver imagined by the average fan, Hanson sells insurance when he's not driving
racing cars.
John Hartwig has been in midget racing five years and has had success in a sport that demands perfec-
tion even from those who don't win. John wrapped up a feature win at Sun Prairie last year and ranked sixth
in the most recent Badger Midget Racing point standings.

Jim Scharmer and Ralph Ermer, you might say, were born to be race drivers. Ralph's dad, Hilbert and
uncle, Ray, built and owned a midget auto in the late 1930s. It's number was 44 and it had an all copper body.
It didn't take the racing gentry long to nickname it "The Copper Kettle." Ermer drove cars he built right after
the Second World War, quitting the driving end of the sport around 1950. Jim's dad, George, drove midgets prior
to the start of the Second World War, but quit driving in 1950. One of George's worst accidents was in a practice
run at Sun Prairie in 1948. George came back to try late model stock car racing in 1949 and 1951. Both of these
young men have had a heritage of speed left to them and they are more than holding their own to maintain it.

Jim Scharmer and Ralph Ermer, you might say, were born to be race drivers. Ralph's dad, Hilbert and
uncle, Ray, built and owned a midget auto in the late 1930s. It's number was 44 and it had an all copper body.
It didn't take the racing gentry long to nickname it "The Copper Kettle." Ermer drove cars he built right after
the Second World War, quitting the driving end of the sport around 1950. Jim's dad, George, drove midgets prior
Located 20 Miles South of Milwaukee or I2 Miles North of the Ilinois-Wisconsin State Line on Highway 45 at
to the start of the Second World War, but quit driving in 1950. One of George's worst accidents was in a practice
run at Sun Prairie in 1948. George came back to try late model stock car racing in 1949 and 1951. Both of these
young men have had a heritage of speed left to them and they are more than holding their own to maintain it.

The car is small but the driver is large. It's the little No. 92 driven by six foot, three inch Bill Haack, who
at around 250 pounds could switch to professional foot-ball any time he chose to. Haack has been driving the
midgets for about five years. He ended the 1964 season with a roll-over in his car at Joliet, Ill. When not racing,
Bill drives a truck. Dable has been racing midget autos since 1959. He's currently driving a car owned by
Wally Champion, Waukesha, who raced hot rods at tracks in this area in the late 1940s.
